4. vector<double>

Yes, and fvar<fvar<var> > and Matrix<fvar<fvar<var> > > and so on.

I think we'll just have to trust that the autodiff
is working because we unit test that independently.

For var, we've customized the autodiff in the functions, so
I think it's fair to test that. I think fvar<double> would
suffice.

The rule is that if there an autodiff type, all the autodiff
types are the same. So I think we can get away with just
testing fvar<double> in addition to var, which given the rule,
should only double the total number of tests if you want to
do it exhaustively.

We could also somehow mock out the vars and fvars using yet
another OperandsAndPartials specialization. That would modularize
the testing for getting the right partials and then dumping out
the right fvar or var.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] fvar distributions!!!
parts:
On Tuesday, June 4, 2013 12:25:12 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
?? I'm lost? What would this be used for?

Here is what it would look like in R code for the standard normal distribution:

# Pick population parameters
# In Stan, these would be var types rather than doubles
# although the the foo_rng() functions only take doubles I think
mu <- 0
sigma <- 1

# Generate large sample from this population
SIMS <- 100000
X <- rnorm(SIMS, mu, sigma)

# Calculate derivatives
# In Stan, this would entail evaluating the gradient of normal_log(X, mu, sigma)
# In R, I just do the gradient analytically
score <- function(x, mu, sigma) c( (x - mu) / sigma^2, (mu^2 - sigma^2 + x^2 - 2 * mu * x) / sigma^3 )
partials <- t(sapply(X, score, mu = mu, sigma = sigma))
colMeans(partials) # small because at the mode

But even better would be to extract the Hessian when normal_log(X, mu, sigma) is evaluated in Stan, get the inverse of the estimated information matrix, and conduct a score test. In R, this is like

I_inv <- diag(c(sigma^2 / SIMS, 2 * sigma^4 / SIMS)) # known analytically
grad <- colSums(partials)
grad %*% I_inv %*% grad # ~ chi-squared with length(grad) degrees of freedom

So, if that test is rejected, then either

-- SIMS was too small
-- there is a rare Type I error
-- the foo_rng function in Stan is wrong
-- the gradient is wrong
-- the Hessian is wrong

But it would be better if this could be automated as much as possible. Definitely drawing the sample, extracting the gradient and Hessian, and conducting the score test is automatable. Setting the population parameters is a bit tricky because different distributions have different numbers of parameters and different restrictions on them.

Ben

parts: On 6/4/13 10:21 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:

> On Tue, Jun 4, 2013 at 10:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
> Good point --- you're absolutely right. And the digamma
> function derivative involves a trigramma. It's turtles all the
> way down.
>
>
> So... how many layers of turtles should we test?
> fvar<fvar<double> >
> fvar<fvar<var> >
>
>
> So for something like fvar<var>, the types to test are (without vectorization):
> fvar<var>, fvar<var>, fvar<var>
> fvar<var>, fvar<var>, var
> fvar<var>, var, fvar<var>
> fvar<var>, var, var
> var, fvar<var>, fvar<var>
> var, fvar<var>, var
> var, var, fvar<var>
>
> But no doubles in there. If it's fvar<fvar<double> >, no doubles, just fvar<double>?

We don't need to mix fvar<var> and var. If there's
an autodiff type, all the autodiff types must be the
same (sort of like vector lengths).

But you do need double. So just replace the bare
var with double and that's what we want to test for
fvar<var>.

I'd say the place to start is with the derivatives
we're going to need for RM-HMC. That's all the
things that are in autodiff.hpp.

I should add some doc for that indicating which
instantiations we need for each function concept.

To get all of these operations with double outputs,
we need these:

autodiff.hpp function autodiff scalar order
----------------------- --------------- -----
gr_tr_mat_times_hessian fvar<fvar<var>> 3
hessian fvar<var> 2
hessian_times_vector fvar<var> 2
gradient_dot_vector var 1
gradient var 1

jacobian var 1
fvar<double> 1

We don't have any use for the Jacobian planned in
the immediate future.

So that means we need tests for

fvar<var>
fvar<fvar<var>>

There is also:

fvar<double>
fvar<fvar<double>>

But we don't really foresee any use for these because
fvar<double> only computes a single derivative (dx1) and
fvar<fvar<double>> only a pair of derivatives and a second
derivative (dx1, dx2 and dx1.dx2).

And it's not just distributions, it's all of our functions
that we need to test.

We don't have second or third order finite diffs for testing.

- Bob

messages.subject: templated trigamma function
parts:
Copyright is for a specific rendering of the algorithm in
code, not for the algorithm itself.

The author of the code you link cites this paper as the
source of the algorithm:

// BE Schneider,
// Algorithm AS 121:
// Trigamma Function,
// Applied Statistics,
// Volume 27, Number 1, pages 97-99, 1978.

So I'd suggest just writing a fresh C++ version based on
the journal algorithm above.

There's also a remark, which I haven't read, that might be
worth reading:

Remark AS R88: A Remark on Algorithm AS 121: The Trigamma Function
Brian J. Francis
Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series C (Applied Statistics)
Vol. 40, No. 3 (1991), pp. 514-515
(article consists of 2 pages)
Published by: Wiley for the Royal Statistical Society

And make sure it's templated and differentiable itself so we can do
higher-order derivatives.

At that point, it's probably not going to look like the other
code very much, so we should be OK on copyright.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] templated trigamma function
parts:
It's in feature/clean_up_fvar in stan/math/functions/trigamma.hpp.


Peter

On 6/11/13 1:00 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Then I think we're OK if you recoded the algorithm in
> C++. Is there a branch with the code in it I can look
> at to compare?
>
> - Bob
>
> On June 11, 2013 12:41:14 PM EDT, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> The paper (http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/apstat/121) looks very similar to the
>> code in the link that I sent earlier.
>>
>>
>> Peter
>>
>> On 6/11/13 12:10 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>>> Of course. I was just pointing out that if he had copied code from
>>> that file, it wouldn't be kosher. A "clean-room" version based on the
>>> paper is perfectly valid.
>>>
>>> Cheers,
>>> Marcus
>>>
>>>
>>> On Tue, Jun 11, 2013 at 12:52 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com
>>> <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>>>
>>> Copyright is for a specific rendering of the algorithm in
>>> code, not for the algorithm itself.
>>>
>>> The author of the code you link cites this paper as the
>>> source of the algorithm:
>>>
>>> // BE Schneider,
>>> // Algorithm AS 121:
>>> // Trigamma Function,
>>> // Applied Statistics,
>>> // Volume 27, Number 1, pages 97-99, 1978.
>>>
>>> So I'd suggest just writing a fresh C++ version based on
>>> the journal algorithm above.
>>>
>>> There's also a remark, which I haven't read, that might be
>>> worth reading:
>>>
>>> Remark AS R88: A Remark on Algorithm AS 121: The Trigamma Function
>>> Brian J. Francis
>>> Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series C (Applied
>>> Statistics)
>>> Vol. 40, No. 3 (1991), pp. 514-515
>>> (article consists of 2 pages)
>>> Published by: Wiley for the Royal Statistical Society
>>>
>>> And make sure it's templated and differentiable itself so we can do
>>> higher-order derivatives.
>>>
>>> At that point, it's probably not going to look like the other
>>> code very much, so we should be OK on copyright.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>
>>> On 6/10/13 11:59 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>>>
>>> That code is LGPLd so cannot be included in Stan.
>>>
>>> Cheers,
>>> Marcus
>>>
>>>
>>> On Mon, Jun 10, 2013 at 11:45 AM, Peter Li
>>> <li.pe...@gmail.com <mailto:li.pe...@gmail.com>
>>> <mailto:li.pe...@gmail.com <mailto:li.pe...@gmail.com>>>
>>> wrote:
>>>
>>> Alright. The version that I've added is based on what
>>> Michael said and
>>> http://people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt/cpp_src/asa121/asa121.cpp
>>> <http://people.sc.fsu.edu/%7Ejburkardt/cpp_src/asa121/asa121.cpp>,
>>> but I'm unsure of how the copyright would work out.
>>>
>>>
>>> Peter
>>>
>>>
>>> On 6/6/13 12:44 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>>
>>> You calculate it the same way you calculate digamma --
>>> you use the recurrence relation to relate phi(x) to phi(x')
>>> where x' >> 1 (10 would be more than enough, I believe
>>> 5 or 6 is recommended in the literature) and then use the
>>> Laurent expansion for phi(x), x >> 1.
>>>
>>>
>>> On Thu, Jun 6, 2013 at 5:41 PM, Bob Carpenter
>>> <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>
>>> <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>>> wrote:
>>>
>>> There's also an implementation in R you could
>>> check out.
>>>
>>> We can't use it directly because of the GPL licensing.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>> On 6/6/13 11:36 AM, Peter Li wrote:
>>>
>>> I'm guessing you mean like how we were able to
>>> use autodiff for a lot of the matrix ops, but the reason I
>>> thought to
>>> implement digamma in the first place was
>>> because the autodiff wasn't working directly when I tried
>>> calling
>>> fvar<fvar<T>>
>>> or fvar<var> of any of the functions involving
>>> the gamma function. I've been looking for a computational
>>> method for
>>> trigamma, but I've had no luck yet.
>>>
>>>
>>> Peter
>>>
>>> On 6/6/13 1:52 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On 6/5/13 6:54 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>>>
>>> Oops. When I added digamma, I didn't
>>> include the correct derivative. I'm not sure how we could add
>>> the trigamma
>>> function--it's not in boost and
>>> doesn't have a closed form.
>>>
>>> Anyone have any ideas?
>>>
>>>
>>> Use autodiff on digamma? Is it templated
>>> well enough
>>> we can do that? You can always test with
>>> finite diffs.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>
>>>
